topics: 🐦 New Perek: The Bird Sin Offering — its life cycle of consecration, pinching, and sprinkling
🚫 Susceptible to Disqualification, Not to Transmitting Impurity — the mishna's precise wording and whose opinion it follows
📈 Rava's 'Higher Standard' — reconciling every tanna's opinion about tevul yom and consecrated food
🩸 Squeezing Out the Remaining Blood — does מיצוי hold up the offering's validity?
📜 A Verse Chain — Leviticus 5:9 tested against both readings, with a parallel challenge from the meal offering

overview.title: 📖 Overview: A New Perek Begins — Chatat HaOf
overview.subtitle: Meilah 8a–8b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The first chapter closes with a final concession — even Rabbi Akiva agrees that sprinkling never actually permits eating meat that left the courtyard, only removes it from me'ilah. The second chapter opens with a new mishna tracing a bird sin offering through three stages: subject to me'ilah from consecration, susceptible to disqualification (but not to transmitting impurity) once its neck is pinched, and subject to piggul/notar/tamei but no longer me'ilah once its blood is sprinkled. The Gemara analyzes precisely whose opinion the mishna follows regarding tevul yom, why a leftover prohibition survives sprinkling, and then pivots to a dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Adda bar Ahava about whether squeezing out the bird's remaining blood is essential to the offering's validity — tracked through two different manuscript traditions of the mishna and a close reading of Leviticus 5:9.

slides.title: 🐦 The Bird Sin Offering's Three Stages
slides.subtitle: What applies to it at each point in its sacrificial life
rows: After the nape of its neck is pinched (מְלִיקָה)
Now susceptible to disqualification via tevul yom, mechusar kippurim, or leaving the blood overnight (linah)
No — no longer subject to me'ilah
Now carries karet liability for piggul, notar, and eating while ritually impure

callout.label: The mishna's structure:
callout.text: Susceptibility to disqualification and liability to karet-level prohibitions both begin only after prior stages are complete — mirroring the 'period of fitness' logic from the first chapter.

slides.title: 🚫 Susceptible to Disqualification — But Can It Transmit Impurity?
slides.subtitle: A precise inference from the mishna's wording

nodes.content: ❓ Mishna says the pinched bird is 'susceptible to disqualification' via tevul yom — does this mean it does NOT transmit impurity onward to other items?
🤔 Whose opinion is this? Abba Shaul: a tevul yom is like first-degree impurity for sacred food; Rabbi Meir: like second-degree; the Rabbis: only disqualifies, doesn't transmit at all
📏 The mishna's wording ('disqualifies' only) fits the Rabbis' view — not Abba Shaul's or Rabbi Meir's

✅ Rava reconciles all views: even Abba Shaul/Rabbi Meir agree that by Torah law a tevul yom merely disqualifies; the Sages added a stringency ('מַעֲלָה') specifically for consecrated items, treating him AS IF first- or second-degree impure

callout.label: Net effect:
callout.text: All three tanna'im can agree with the mishna's basic Torah-law statement; their dispute is really about a rabbinic stringency layered on top.

slides.title: 🍖 No Me'ilah, But Still Forbidden to Eat
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Ḥanina resolves the same puzzle seen on the previous daf
slides.hebrewSource: לַיּוֹצְאִין, וְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא הִיא, דְּאָמַר זְרִיקָה מוֹעֶלֶת לַיּוֹצֵא, דְּלָאו בַּת אֲכִילָה הִיא
slides.label: The resolution:
slides.text: The mishna says that after sprinkling, one is no longer liable for me'ilah — implying, if read strictly, that the meat is now simply permitted, like ordinary priestly property. But an unstated prohibition on eating it remains. Rabbi Ḥanina explains: this is meat that left the permitted eating area before the blood was sprinkled. Per Rabbi Akiva's rule, sprinkling still removes such meat from me'ilah, but it never actually becomes fit to eat — sprinkling protects it from misuse without restoring its edibility.

slides.title: 🩸 Rav Huna vs. Rav Adda bar Ahava: Is Squeezing Essential?
slides.subtitle: Two versions of the mishna's final phrase drive the dispute

lines.speaker: Rav Huna
lines.text: Failure to squeeze out the bird sin offering's remaining blood (מִיצּוּי) does NOT invalidate the offering — his version of the mishna reads 'once its blood was sprinkled' (הוּזָּה דָּמָהּ).

lines.speaker: Rav Adda bar Ahava
lines.text: Squeezing out the remaining blood DOES invalidate the offering if omitted — his version reads 'once its blood was squeezed out' (מִיצָּה דָּמָהּ).

lines.speaker: Challenge
lines.text: Leviticus 5:9 states: 'the remainder of the blood shall be squeezed out at the base of the altar, it is a sin offering' — this phrasing seems to make squeezing essential, supporting Rav Adda bar Ahava.

lines.speaker: Rav Huna's answer
lines.text: Per the school of Rabbi Yishmael: the verse means only if blood remains, squeeze it out — not that blood must remain to be squeezed. 'It is a sin offering' refers back to the sprinkling clause, not the squeezing clause.

callout.label: Stakes:
callout.text: If squeezing is not essential, a bird sin offering is valid — and exits me'ilah — from the moment of sprinkling alone.

slides.title: 📜 Testing the Verse — and a Parallel From the Meal Offering
slides.subtitle: Does 'the remainder shall be squeezed out' set a requirement or just a contingency?

steps.content: 1️⃣ Leviticus 5:9: 'the remainder of the blood shall be squeezed out at the base of the altar, it is a sin offering'
2️⃣ Rav Huna reads it (via Beit Rabbi Yishmael) as conditional: IF blood remains, squeeze it — no requirement that blood must remain
3️⃣ Rav Aḥa, son of Rava, challenges Rav Ashi: doesn't the same logic apply to the meal offering's leftover verse — 'that which is left (וְהַנּוֹתֶרֶת) shall be Aaron's' (Lev. 2:3)?
4️⃣ Should that too mean only 'IF something remains, it goes to the priests' — with no requirement that anything remain at all?

callout.label: To be continued:
callout.text: This parallel challenge about the meal offering's leftovers is the question that carries directly into the next daf.

summary.principle: The bird sin offering moves through me'ilah, disqualification-susceptibility, and finally piggul/notar/tamei liability in sequence, and the dispute over whether squeezing out its remaining blood is essential turns entirely on how to read the 'conditional versus mandatory' structure of Leviticus 5:9.

flowSteps.content: 🐦 Bird sin offering: me'ilah from consecration → disqualification-susceptible from pinching → piggul/notar/tamei from sprinkling
🚫 'Susceptible to disqualification' (not impurity) fits the Rabbis; Rava reconciles all views via a rabbinic stringency

columns.content: 🍖 No me'ilah after sprinkling, yet still forbidden — meat that left, per Rabbi Akiva (Rabbi Ḥanina)
🩸 Rav Huna vs. Rav Adda bar Ahava: is squeezing out remaining blood essential to validity?

flowSteps.content: 📜 Leviticus 5:9 read conditionally (Beit R' Yishmael) to favor Rav Huna — but the same logic is challenged via the meal offering's leftover verse
🎓 Key Principle: a verse's 'and the remainder shall be...' can describe a contingency, not a requirement — the debate is whether that reading holds consistently across sacrifices

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, at what point does a bird sin offering stop being subject to me'ilah?
o: From the moment it is consecrated
Once the nape of its neck is pinched
Once its blood is sprinkled
It is never subject to me'ilah
quiz.e: The mishna states that once the blood is sprinkled, one is liable for piggul, notar, and tamei but no longer for me'ilah, since the meat becomes permitted to the priests.

quiz.q: How does Rava reconcile the mishna's wording (that a tevul yom only disqualifies, does not transmit impurity) with the opinions of Abba Shaul and Rabbi Meir, who seem to say a tevul yom does transmit impurity?
o: He says the mishna is not authoritative
He explains that by Torah law all agree a tevul yom only disqualifies; Abba Shaul and Rabbi Meir describe a rabbinic stringency added specifically for consecrated items
He says Abba Shaul and Rabbi Meir are discussing a different kind of impurity entirely
He says the mishna follows Rabbi Meir, not the Rabbis
quiz.e: Rava harmonizes the positions by saying the underlying Torah law is the same for everyone; the dispute is only about an additional rabbinic stringency (מעלה) applied to sacred food.

quiz.q: Why, according to Rabbi Ḥanina, does a prohibition on eating survive even though the mishna says there is no more me'ilah after the blood is sprinkled?
o: Because the meat is still fully consecrated to God
Because the case refers to meat that left the permitted eating area before sprinkling — following Rabbi Akiva, sprinkling removes it from me'ilah but does not restore its fitness to be eaten
Because priests are never permitted to eat sin offerings
Because the blood was never actually sprinkled
quiz.e: Rabbi Ḥanina explains this using Rabbi Akiva's rule: sprinkling can exempt meat that already left the eating area from me'ilah, but that meat still isn't fit for consumption.

quiz.q: What is the core dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Adda bar Ahava regarding a bird sin offering's remaining blood?
o: Whether the blood may be sprinkled twice
Whether squeezing out (מיצוי) the remaining blood at the base of the altar is essential to the offering's validity
Whether the bird may be eaten raw
Whether the offering requires two priests
quiz.e: Rav Huna holds that failing to squeeze out the remaining blood does not invalidate the offering, while Rav Adda bar Ahava holds that it does — based on two different versions of the mishna's text.

quiz.q: How does Rav Huna, following the school of Rabbi Yishmael, explain the verse 'the remainder of the blood shall be squeezed out... it is a sin offering' (Leviticus 5:9)?
o: The verse requires that blood must always remain to be squeezed out
The verse means only that IF blood remains, it must be squeezed out — there is no requirement that blood remain in the first place, and 'it is a sin offering' refers back to the sprinkling clause
The verse has nothing to do with the bird sin offering
The verse proves that squeezing is always essential
quiz.e: Rav Huna reads the verse as conditional rather than mandatory, so the offering's validity depends on sprinkling, not on squeezing out any remaining blood.
